H1.text: A quarter turn of a bicycle wheel is ninety degrees. A full turn is three hundred and sixty.

H2.text: But who chose three hundred and sixty? Not the wheel. People did.

H3.text: Aarav thought about this while riding to college today.

H4.text: His wheel rolls along the road as it turns. Could the road tell us how far it turned?

H5.text: It can. That idea is called the radian, and it opens a new chapter: Chapter 3, Trigonometric Functions.

G2.text: An angle is a measure of rotation. A ray turns about its starting point.

G3.text: The ray starts on the initial side. Where it stops is the terminal side. The point it turns about is the vertex.

G4.text: Watch it turn. The more it rotates, the bigger the angle. Now we need a unit to count it.

D1.text: The first unit is the degree.

D2.text: Cut one full turn into three hundred and sixty equal slices. One slice is one degree.

D3.text: For finer work, one degree is cut into sixty minutes, and one minute into sixty seconds.

D4.text: Three hundred and sixty splits evenly in many ways. But it is still a number people chose.

K1.text: Quick one. Can an angle be bigger than three hundred and sixty degrees? Pause and think.

K2.text: Yes! The ray can keep turning. One full turn plus sixty degrees more is four hundred and twenty degrees.

R1.text: Now the second unit. This one comes from the circle itself.

R2.text: Take a circle whose radius is one unit. We call it a unit circle.

R3.text: Mark an arc on its rim that is also one unit long.

R4.text: The angle this arc makes at the centre is one radian.

R5.text: In any circle, when the arc is as long as the radius, the angle is one radian.

R6.text: Now watch. Lay the radius around the rim, again and again. One, two, three, four, five, six.

R7.text: Six radii fit, and a small gap is left. All the way round is about six point two eight radians. That number is two pi.

V1.text: So how do we find the angle for any arc? Four small steps.

V2.text: Step one. An arc as long as the radius makes one radian.

V3.text: Step two. Equal arcs make equal angles at the centre. So an arc two radii long makes two radians.

V4.text: Step three. So the angle in radians is how many radii fit in the arc. Theta equals l over r.

V6.text: Step four. Multiply both sides by r. The arc length l equals r times theta.

V7.text: Check it on a full turn. The arc is the whole rim, two pi r. Divide by r, and theta is two pi.

T1.text: Remember this. One radian is the angle where the arc equals the radius.

S1.text: Side by side. Degrees cut a full turn into three hundred and sixty parts. That number was chosen by people.

S2.text: Radians count the arc in radii. A full turn is two pi, about six point two eight. That number comes from the circle.

S3.text: A radian is a length divided by a length, so it has no real unit. When an angle has no unit written, it is in radians.

S4.text: Now you try. A tiny wheel and a giant wheel each roll an arc equal to their own radius. Which one turns through the bigger angle? Pause and think.

S5.text: Neither! Both turn exactly one radian. The radian does not care how big the circle is.

W2.text: Aarav's wheel has a radius of thirty five centimetres. His bicycle rolls forward one metre. Through what angle, in radians, does the wheel turn?

W3.text: Step one. When a wheel rolls without slipping, the road it covers equals the arc that touched the road. So l is one metre.

W4.text: Step two. Use the same units. One metre is one hundred centimetres.

W5.text: Step three. Theta equals l over r, which is one hundred over thirty five.

W6.text: Step four. That is twenty over seven, about two point eight six radians.

W7.text: That is less than half of two pi, so the wheel turned a little less than half a turn.

X2.text: Arc length for one full turn, radius ten centimetres. Many students write l equals ten times three hundred and sixty.

X3.text: But l equals r theta needs theta in radians. A full turn is two pi, so l is ten times two pi, about sixty two point eight centimetres.

J1.text: Where is this asked? In the PUC board exams: given an arc and a radius, find the angle in radians, or the other way round.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Find theta in radians. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. Five by four.

A2.text: The perimeter of a sector is two radii plus the arc. So two r plus l equals twenty six.

A3.text: The arc is two more than the radius, so l is r plus two. Then three r plus two is twenty six, and r is eight.

A4.text: So l is ten. Theta is l over r, ten over eight, which is five by four radians.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. How many degrees are there in two full turns?

Y3.text: Two. An arc of fifteen centimetres sits on a circle of radius five. What is the angle in radians?

Y4.text: Three. Why is one radian the same size in every circle?

N1.text: Next time: half a wheel turn is one hundred and eighty degrees, and also pi radians. So how do we switch between the two?
